McLeroy of'). adversarial_test_results.prompt:
When the freighter Northern Light docked at Pier Nine just after dawn, the harbormaster had already been on the telephone for an hour. The manifest listed timber, coal, and a shipment of machine parts bound for the mills upstream, and the crew had spent most of the crossing repairing a pump that failed somewhere off the coast of Labrador. Weather reports from the night before warned of a squall moving east, so the captain ordered the hatches sealed and the deckhands to double-check the mooring lines. By seven the gangway was down and the first trucks were already idling on the quay, their drivers drinking coffee from paper cups while they waited for the paperwork to clear.

None of it went smoothly. A customs officer named Beaudry spent the morning arguing with the shipping agent about a discrepancy in the bill of lading, and the argument delayed the unloading by two hours. When the crane finally swung into position, one of the slings snapped and a pallet of roofing tiles crashed onto the concrete, scattering shards across thirty feet of dock. The foreman swore, wrote something in his notebook, and sent a boy to fetch a broom. In the office above the warehouse a clerk named Mrs. Doucet typed the same invoice three times because the carbon paper kept tearing, and each time she complained that the typewriter needed a new ribbon. Downstairs, two dockworkers argued about whether the crane operator had been drinking, and the argument ended only when the whistle blew for lunch.

The afternoon brought a lull. The squall never arrived, the wind dropped, and the men ate sandwiches on the seawall while gulls wheeled overhead. Someone produced a radio and they listened to a ball game from Boston, the reception fading in and out with every passing truck. A young stevedore named Arseneau told a long story about a cousin who had shipped out on a whaler and come back with a tattoo of an anchor and a limp that he refused to explain. The others laughed and threw crusts at the gulls, and for a while the only sounds were the water against the pilings and the crackle of the radio.

It was nearly four when the second truck arrived from the depot, and with it a police escort and a great deal of shouting. Two officers climbed out and spoke quietly with the foreman, who nodded and pointed toward the end of the pier where the last of the cargo sat under a canvas tarp. The crew had been told nothing, and the speculation was wild: someone said it was medical supplies, someone else insisted it was contraband seized in Halifax, and a third man swore he had seen the same crates loaded in Boston under armed guard. In the end it was only what the manifest had promised all along, though nobody had thought to mention it aloud.
